# os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/os_display/

## Expand description

Formatters for printing filenames and other strings in a terminal, with attention paid to special characters and invalid unicode.

They will wrap quotes around them and add the necessary escapes to make them copy/paste-able into a shell.

The [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html) trait adds

`quote` and `maybe_quote` methods to string
types. The [type has constructors for more explicit control.](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)

`Quoted`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;
let path = Path::new("foo/bar.baz");
// Found file 'foo/bar.baz'
println!("Found file {}", path.quote());
// foo/bar.baz: Not found
println!("{}: Not found", path.maybe_quote());
```
If the `windows`/`unix` features are enabled:

```
use os_display::Quoted;
// "foo`nbar"
println!("{}", Quoted::windows("foo\nbar"));
// $'foo\nbar'
println!("{}", Quoted::unix("foo\nbar"));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)
- A wrapper around string types for displaying with quoting and escaping applied.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html)
- An extension trait to apply quoting to strings.

# os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/os_display/0.1.4/os_display/

## Expand description

Formatters for printing filenames and other strings in a terminal, with attention paid to special characters and invalid unicode.

They will wrap quotes around them and add the necessary escapes to make them copy/paste-able into a shell.

The [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html) trait adds

`quote` and `maybe_quote` methods to string
types. The [type has constructors for more explicit control.](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)

`Quoted`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;

use os_display::Quoted;

# os_display 0.1.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/os_display/latest

`os_display`

This crate quotes strings so that they can be copy/pasted in the terminal.

```
use os_display::Quotable;
"filename".quote() → 'filename'
"foo'bar".quote() → "foo'bar"
"foo\u{1B}".quote() → $'foo\x1B'
"ihavenospaces".maybe_quote() → ihavenospaces
"i do have spaces".maybe_quote() → 'i do have spaces'
```
This deals with a number of problems:

-
Strings can have control codes that mess up the message or the whole terminal.
-
Whitespace and special characters must be quoted or escaped to be used in a shell command.
-
`OsString`s and`Path`s can contain invalid Unicode (which even`Path::display`

Values are rendered so that they can always be pasted back into a shell without information loss.

On Unix (and other platforms) values are quoted using bash/ksh syntax, while on Windows PowerShell syntax is used.

## When should I use this?

This crate is especially useful for command line programs that deal with arbitrary filenames or other "dirty" text. `ls` for example is the very tool you use to find odd filenames, so it's nice if it displays them well. This is why it's used in [ uutils](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils).

Another use case is printing commands for the user to run. [ xh](https://github.com/ducaale/xh) has a mode that prints

`curl` commands, using this crate to make them pretty and copy/pastable on both Unix and Windows.Any program that prints text that the user might want to paste into a terminal can get some use out of this.

Most programs get along fine without it. You likely don't strictly need it, but you may find it a nice improvement.

## Usage

Import the [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/os_display/latest/os_display/trait.Quotable.html) trait:

```
use Quotable;
```
This adds two methods to the common string types (including `OsStr`): `.quote()` and `.maybe_quote()`. They return `Quoted`, a wrapper with a custom `Display` implementation.

`.quote()` always puts quotes around the text:

```
// Found file 'filename'
println!;
// Found file "foo'bar"
println!;
// Unix: Found file $'foo\nbar'
// Windows: Found file "foo`nbar"
println!;
```
`.maybe_quote()` only adds them if necessary because of whitespace or special characters:

```
// filename: Not found
println!;
// 'foo bar': Not found
println!;
// '*?$': Not found
println!;
```
`.quote()` is best used inside longer sentences while `.maybe_quote()` can be used for text that's already separated some other way, like by a colon. This is the convention of many GNU programs.

## Limitations

- Unicode may be quoted but only control characters are escaped. The printed text can still look weird, and a few (buggy) terminals drop certain characters.
- This library should **not**be used to interpolate text into shell scripts. It's designed for readability, not absolute safety. Consider using the`shell-escape`
- The output is not compatible with every single shell.
- [Old versions of PowerShell treat quotes differently in arguments to external commands](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6714165). This library defaults to the modern behavior. The- `Quoted::external()`method toggles legacy quoting.
- I'm not a Unicode expert. The first release of this crate had multiple oversights and there may be more.

## Invalid unicode

On Unix:

```
use OsStr;
use OsStrExt;
// \xFF makes this invalid UTF-8, so to_str() would fail
let bad_string = from_bytes;
assert_eq!;
```
On Windows:

```
use OsString;
use OsStringExt;
// 0xD800 is an unpaired surrogate, making this invalid UTF-16
let bad_string = from_wide;
assert_eq!;
```
## Zero-width unicode

Some codepoints are zero-width. They can make a string invisible, or they can make it hard to select. GNU tools struggle with this:

```
$ wc $'\u200b'
wc: : No such file or directory
```
`os_display` adds quotes in such cases:

```
assert_eq!;
```
It still misleadingly looks like `''` when printed, but it's possible to copy and paste it and get the right result.

## Bidirectional unicode

A carefully-crafted string can move part of itself to the end of the line:

```
$ wc $'filename\u202E\u2066 [This does not belong!]\u2069\u2066'
wc: 'filename': No such file or directory [This does not belong!]
```
This is known as a [ Trojan Source](https://trojansource.codes/) attack. It uses control codes for bidirectional text.

`os_display` escapes those control codes if they're not properly terminated.

## Feature flags

By default you can only use the current platform's quoting style. That's appropriate most of the time.

`windows`/`unix`

The `windows` and `unix` optional features can be enabled to add constructors to `Quoted`.

`Quoted::unix("some string")` will quote with bash/ksh syntax no matter the platform, and `Quoted::windows("etc")` uses PowerShell syntax.

`Quoted::unix_raw` and `Quoted::windows_raw` take `&[u8]` (for malformed UTF-8) and `&[u16]` (for malformed UTF-16), respectively.

`native`

The `native` feature (enabled by default) is required for the `Quotable` trait and the `Quoted::native(&str)` and `Quoted::native_raw(&OsStr)` constructors. If it's not enabled then the quoting style has to be chosen explicitly.

`alloc`/`std`

This crate is `no_std`-compatible if the `alloc` and/or `std` features are disabled.

The `std` feature is required to quote `OsStr`s. The `alloc` feature is required for `Quoted::windows_raw`.

## Alternative constructors

`Quoted` has constructors for specific styles as well as `Quoted::native()` and `Quoted::native_raw()`. These can be used as an alternative to the `Quotable` trait if you prefer boring functions.

By default quotes are always added. To get behavior like `.maybe_quote()` use the `.force()` method:

```
println!;
```
## Testing

The Unix implementation has been [fuzzed](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz) against bash, zsh, mksh, ksh93 and busybox to ensure all output is interpreted back as the original string. It has been fuzzed to a more limited extent against fish, dash, tcsh, posh, and yash (which don't support all of the required syntax).

The PowerShell implementation has been fuzzed against PowerShell Core 7.1.4 running on Linux.

Both implementations have been fuzzed to test their protection against Trojan Source attacks.

## Acknowledgments

This library is modeled after the quoting done by [Gnulib](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnulib/) as seen in the GNU coreutils. The behavior is not identical, however:

- GNU uses octal escapes, like `\377`instead of`\xFF`.
- GNU eagerly switches quoting style midway through, like `''$'\n''xyz'`instead of`$'\nxyz'`.`os_display`avoids this unless necessary.
- GNU escapes unassigned codepoints instead of leaving their handling up to the terminal.
- GNU doesn't handle zero-width codepoints specially.

The first version of this code was written for the [uutils project](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils). The feedback and the opportunity to use it in a large codebase were helpful.

# unicode_width - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unicode-width/^0.2.0/

## Expand description

Determine displayed width of `char` and `str` types according to
[Unicode Standard Annex #11](http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr11/)
and other portions of the Unicode standard.
See the [Rules for determining width](https://docs.rs#rules-for-determining-width) section
for the exact rules.

This crate is `#![no_std]`.

```
use unicode_width::UnicodeWidthStr;
let teststr = "Ｈｅｌｌｏ, ｗｏｒｌｄ!";
let width = UnicodeWidthStr::width(teststr);
println!("{}", teststr);
println!("The above string is {} columns wide.", width);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cjk-feature-flag)`"cjk"` feature flag

This crate has one Cargo feature flag, `"cjk"`
(enabled by default).
It enables the [ UnicodeWidthChar::width_cjk](https://docs.rs/trait.UnicodeWidthChar.html#tymethod.width_cjk)
and

[, which perform an alternate width calculation more suited to CJK contexts. The flag also unseals the](https://docs.rs/trait.UnicodeWidthStr.html#tymethod.width_cjk)

`UnicodeWidthStr::width_cjk`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.UnicodeWidthChar.html)

`UnicodeWidthChar`[traits.](https://docs.rs/trait.UnicodeWidthStr.html)

`UnicodeWidthStr`Disabling the flag (with `no_default_features` in `Cargo.toml`)
will reduce the amount of static data needed by the crate.

```
use unicode_width::UnicodeWidthStr;
let teststr = "“𘀀”";
assert_eq!(teststr.width(), 4);
#[cfg(feature = "cjk")]
assert_eq!(teststr.width_cjk(), 6);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rules-for-determining-width)Rules for determining width

This crate currently uses the following rules to determine the width of a character or string, in order of decreasing precedence. These may be tweaked in the future.

- In the following cases, the width of a string differs from the sum of the widths of its constituent characters:
- The sequence `"\r\n"`has width 1.
- Emoji-specific ligatures:
- Well-formed, fully-qualified [emoji ZWJ sequences](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr51/#def_emoji_sequence)have width 2.
- [Emoji modifier sequences](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr51/#def_emoji_modifier_sequence)have width 2.
- [Emoji presentation sequences](https://unicode.org/reports/tr51/#def_emoji_presentation_sequence)have width 2.
- Outside of an East Asian context, [text presentation sequences](https://unicode.org/reports/tr51/#def_text_presentation_sequence)have width 1 if their base character:- Has the `Emoji_Presentation`
- Is not in the [Enclosed Ideographic Supplement](https://unicode.org/charts/nameslist/n_1F200.html)block.

- Has the

- Well-formed, fully-qualified
- `'\u{2018}'`,- `'\u{2019}'`,- `'\u{201C}'`, and- `'\u{201D}'`
- Script-specific ligatures:
- For all the following ligatures, the insertion of any number of [default-ignorable](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-5/#G40095)[combining marks](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-3/#G30602)anywhere in the sequence will not change the total width. In addition, for all non-Arabic ligatures, the insertion of any number of`'\u{200D}'`ZERO WIDTH JOINER
- [Arabic](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-9/#G7480)- `Joining_Group`- `=Lam`, followed by any number of characters with- `Joining_Type`- `=Transparent`, followed by one character with- `Joining_Group`- `=Alef`, has total width 1. For example:- `لا`,- `لآ`,- `ڸا`,- `لٟٞأ`
- [Buginese](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-17/#G26743)- `"\u{1A15}\u{1A17}\u{200D}\u{1A10}"`(<a, -i> ya,- `ᨕᨗᨐ`) has total width 1.
- [Hebrew](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-9/#G6528)- `"א\u{200D}ל"`(Alef-Lamed,- `אל`) has total width 1.
- [Khmer](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-16/#G64642)- `'\u{17D2}'`followed by a character in- `'\u{1780}'..='\u{1782}' | '\u{1784}'..='\u{1787}' | '\u{1789}'..='\u{178C}' | '\u{178E}'..='\u{1793}' | '\u{1795}'..='\u{1798}' | '\u{179B}'..='\u{179D}' | '\u{17A0}' | '\u{17A2}' | '\u{17A7}' | '\u{17AB}'..='\u{17AC}' | '\u{17AF}'`have width 0.
- [Kirat Rai](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-13/#G746409)- `'\u{16D68}'`,- `'\u{16D69}'`, or- `'\u{16D6A}'`has total width 1.
- [Lisu](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-18/#G44587)- `'\u{A4F8}'..='\u{A4FB}'`followed by a character in the range- `'\u{A4FC}'..='\u{A4FD}'`have width 1. For example:- `ꓹꓼ`
- [Old Turkic](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-14/#G41975)- `"\u{10C32}\u{200D}\u{10C03}"`(- `𐰲𐰃`) has total width 1.
- [Tifinagh](http://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-19/#G43184)- `'\u{2D31}'..='\u{2D65}' | '\u{2D6F}'`, followed by either- `'\u{2D7F}'`TIFINAGH CONSONANT JOINER- `'\u{200D}'`, followed by another Tifinangh consonant, has total width 1. For example:- `ⵏ⵿ⴾ`

- For all the following ligatures, the insertion of any number of

- `'\u{A8FA}'`DEVANAGARI CARET

- Characters fulfilling all of the following conditions have width 2 in an East Asian context, and width 1 otherwise:

- Has a canonical decomposition to an `Ambiguous``'\u{0338}'`COMBINING LONG SOLIDUS OVERLAY
- Is `'\u{0387}'`GREEK ANO TELEIA

- Has an

- Fulfills one of the following conditions:
- All other characters have width 1.

[§](https://docs.rs#canonical-equivalence)Canonical equivalence

Canonically equivalent strings are assigned the same width (CJK and non-CJK).

# os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/os_display/latest/target-redirect/os_display/

## Expand description

Formatters for printing filenames and other strings in a terminal, with attention paid to special characters and invalid unicode.

They will wrap quotes around them and add the necessary escapes to make them copy/paste-able into a shell.

The [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html) trait adds

`quote` and `maybe_quote` methods to string
types. The [type has constructors for more explicit control.](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)

`Quoted`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;
let path = Path::new("foo/bar.baz");
// Found file 'foo/bar.baz'
println!("Found file {}", path.quote());
// foo/bar.baz: Not found
println!("{}: Not found", path.maybe_quote());
```
If the `windows`/`unix` features are enabled:

```
use os_display::Quoted;
// "foo`nbar"
println!("{}", Quoted::windows("foo\nbar"));
// $'foo\nbar'
println!("{}", Quoted::unix("foo\nbar"));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)
- A wrapper around string types for displaying with quoting and escaping applied.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# facett_icebergview - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-icebergview/0.1.10/facett_icebergview/

## Expand description

**facett-icebergview** — browse **and time-travel** one Iceberg table, drawn
from **Arrow  RecordBatches**. The component is

*engine-agnostic*: you hand it, per Iceberg snapshot, the snapshot’s metadata + its materialized Arrow frame; it renders a

**snapshot picker**(newest-first, showing snapshot id / timestamp / row-count) over a virtualized,

**paged**row grid (the rows come from

[, built from the batch via](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[). Selecting a snapshot loads](https://docs.rs/facett-arrow/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_arrow/index.html)

`facett_arrow`*that*snapshot’s frame — time travel.

Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html) (

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json`), so it drops into a `FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through
`facett_core::harness`: drive [/](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.select_snapshot)

`IcebergView::select_snapshot`[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.set_page)

`IcebergView::set_page``state_json` (the current snapshot, the snapshot list,
and the visible rows all change). `state_json` exposes:- `table`— the table name,
- `snapshots`— every snapshot newest-first (- `id`,- `timestamp_ms`,- `rows`),
- `current`— the selected snapshot id,
- `total_rows`/- `page`/- `page_size`/- `visible_rows`— the paged view.

**Why not just  facett-table?** A table viewer shows

*one*frame. This adds the Iceberg dimension — the history of snapshots and the control to scrub between them — which is the whole point of a lakehouse table browser. The adapter that

*fills*it from a real catalog (skade) lives host-side (korp / nornir) so this crate never takes a hard catalog/engine dependency.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iceberg](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html)- View
- A browse + time-travel viewer for one Iceberg table.
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.Snapshot.html)
- One snapshot paired with the Arrow frame that materializes it. The frame is a
`Vec<RecordBatch>`exactly as a scan returns it;`IcebergView`concatenates the rows into a paged`Table`
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.SnapshotMeta.html)- Meta
- One Iceberg snapshot’s identity, for the picker + `state_json`. Mirrors what`iceberg::spec::Snapshot`exposes (`snapshot_id()`/`timestamp_ms()`) plus a row count the host computes (scan count, or the snapshot summary’s`total-records`).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE.html)- PAGE_ - SIZE
- Default rows shown per page (the Table is virtualized, but paging keeps a huge
snapshot from being cell-formatted all at once and makes `visible_rows`meaningful for headless assertions).

---

# facett_warehousedeck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-warehousedeck/0.1.10/facett_warehousedeck/

## Expand description

**facett-warehousedeck** — a multi-pane **dashboard over a lakehouse
warehouse**. It views the warehouse as **many components at once**: several
**3D graphs** (call graph, dependency graph, world-delta, release lineage,
SBOM/vuln) **plus** grids and charts, all visible simultaneously in a wall.

It is built **entirely from existing facett widgets** — it never reimplements
a viewer. Each pane is one of:
[ facett_graph3d::Graph3D](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/struct.Graph3D.html) ·

[/](https://docs.rs/facett-grid/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_grid/struct.Grid.html)

`facett_grid::Grid`[·](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[, composed inside a](https://docs.rs/facett-plot/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_plot/struct.PlotView.html)

`facett_plot::PlotView`[. The deck is rendered in](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html)

`facett_core::FacetDeck`**Wall**mode (

[) so every pane (and thus several](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.wall_ui)

`FacetDeck::wall_ui``Graph3D` instances) draws at once; a **Focus**mode falls back to the deck’s tabbed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.ui)

`FacetDeck::ui`[§](https://docs.rs#engine-agnostic)Engine-agnostic

Like the rest of facett, this crate takes **data, not a catalog**: a host
(nornir’s viz) opens its Iceberg warehouse, reads each table, maps the rows to
a [ PaneData](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html) view-model, and hands them in. This crate never depends on
iceberg/skade/nornir.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-registry-table--view-kind)The registry (table → view-kind)

[ WarehouseRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html) maps a

**table name**to the

[it should render as, so adding a table is one](https://docs.rs/enum.ViewKind.html)

`ViewKind``register(...)` line. The host queries the
registry to decide which [to build for a table; explicit join-panes (e.g. the call graph from](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html)

`PaneData``call_edges`×`symbol_facts`) are added directly.[§](https://docs.rs#robot-testable)Robot-testable

[ WarehouseDeck](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html) is itself a

[, so it drops into nornir’s viz and is headless-assertable.](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`[exposes](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html#method.state_json)

`WarehouseDeck::state_json``pane_count`,
per-kind counts (`graph3d_count`, `grid_count`, …), and a `panes` array
carrying each pane’s `nodes`/`edges`/`rows`/`series`, plus the composed deck
state (whose `trace.ran` lists `deck.wall:<title>` for every pane that drew).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chart](https://docs.rs/struct.ChartSpec.html)- Spec
- A chart view-model: named `(x, y)`series + the chart kind. Maps onto`PlotView`
- [Color32](https://docs.rs/struct.Color32.html)
- This format is used for space-efficient color representation (32 bits).
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphSpec.html)- Spec
- A 3D-graph view-model: `(label, color)`nodes + index edges + a layout. Maps directly onto`Graph3D::new`
- [Pane](https://docs.rs/struct.PaneInfo.html)- Info
- Per-pane metadata, mirrored into `state_json`for headless assertions.
- [Warehouse](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html)- Deck
- A `FacetDeck``Facet`
- [Warehouse](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html)- Registry
- **table name →**— the registry that makes adding a table trivial. The host queries- `ViewKind`- `kind_for`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- Deck render layout.

- 3D placement strategies (positions are filled by `Graph3D::layout`

- [Plot](https://docs.rs/enum.PlotKind.html)- Kind

- How a warehouse table is rendered. The registry maps each table to one of
these; `PaneData`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Facet](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)
- The facett **component contract**. Every facet — graph, map, pipeline, table, the ported nornir viewers — implements this, so consumers (korp, nornir, …) compose them uniformly*and*get headless robot-testing for free.

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-riemann/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann/

## Expand description

Neo-Riemannian / functional triad naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Riemannian naming school: it labels a triad by its
functional quality relative to its root, distinguishing a major triad (`T`,
upper-case for the major tonic function) from a minor triad (`t`,
lower-case). [ label_riemann](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html) rotates the pitch-class set so the root sits at
zero and matches the major or minor triad signature; non-triadic sets return

`None`.## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [label_](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html)- riemann
- Labels `mask`as a major (`T`) or minor (`t`) triad relative to its root.

# facett_security - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-security/0.1.10/facett_security/

## Expand description

**facett-security** — a software-supply-chain **security report** view: the
**verdict** (Pass / Warn / Block), the **findings** list (id · severity ·
package · advisory · fix) with **severity / EPSS / KEV** columns, and a
secondary **CVE / advisory** reference table. It is the UI *twin* of
[modgunn](https://codeberg.org/nordisk/modgunn)’s scan output — the gate that
decides whether an artifact may be served / promoted.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-on-purpose-no-modgunn-dependency)Generic on purpose (no modgunn dependency)

facett MUST NOT couple to the modgunn crate. So this crate carries its **own**
plain, serializable structs — [ Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)

`Severity`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)

`Finding`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`[— whose shape](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)

`SecurityReport`**mirrors**so a consumer (nornir-viz / holger-ui) maps the two

`modgunn::core`**1:1**with no glue:

| facett-security | modgunn::core |
|---|---|
| (Pass/Warn/Block)`Verdict` | `Decision`(Pass/Warn/Block) — same`Ord` |
| (Info…Critical)`Severity` | `Severity`(Info…Critical) — same`Ord` |
| `Finding``{id,severity,…}` | `Finding``{id,severity,summary}`(superset) |
| `Artifact` | `ArtifactRef` |
| `SecurityReport` | `Verdict`(the whole cacheable result) |

[ Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html) is a

**superset**: modgunn’s three fields map straight in, and the richer scan columns the UI wants (

`package`, `advisory`, `fix`, `epss`, `kev`)
are optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has and leaves the rest defaulted.[§](https://docs.rs#fc-compliance-the-component-contract)FC compliance (the component contract)

- **FC-1 / FC-3**— all observable state lives in one serializable- `SecurityState`- `Serialize`/- `Deserialize`/- `Clone`/- `PartialEq`), read back via- `SecurityView::state`
- **FC-2 / FC-9**— every input is a- `Msg`- `SecurityView::update`- `render`- `&self`that paints and- *returns*the- `Msg`- `Facet::ui`
- **FC-4**— the painted verdict pill emits an AccessKit node; every finding row / CVE row is a selectable, labelled, value-carrying node.
- **FC-5**— rows are keyed off the finding- **id**(a stable domain key), never a loop index.
- **FC-6**— pure egui + painter, renders headlessly (the deck robot path).
- **FC-7**— no ambient clock / RNG / animation: the scan time is an- *injected*host-stamped string (- `SecurityReport::scanned_at`
- **FC-8**— the view does no I/O;- `SecurityView::is_idle`- `SecurityView::update`- `Vec<Effect>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- The artifact a verdict is about (content-addressed). Mirrors
`modgunn::core::ArtifactRef`.
- [Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)
- One thing the scanner found. `id`,`severity`,`summary`map straight from`modgunn::core::Finding`; the rest are the richer scan columns the UI shows (all optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has).
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)- Report
- The cacheable scan result: the verdict + its findings + the keys it was
computed against. The plain data a host hands the view; mirrors the whole of
`modgunn::core::Verdict`.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityState.html)- State
- **All**observable state for the view (FC-1 / FC-3): the report plus the UI state (the drilled-in finding, the severity floor filter, and the zoom). Fully serializable so a caller reads it back at any frame boundary.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityView.html)- View
- The `Facet``SecurityReport`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Effect](https://docs.rs/enum.Effect.html)
- Side work as data (FC-8). The view does no I/O, so this is uninhabited — it exists to make the “no pending effects” contract explicit and type-checked.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Every input the view accepts (FC-2). The **only**legal way to mutate`SecurityState``Debug`+`Clone`.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Finding severity (declaration order = ascending, so the worst finding is the
`max()`). Mirrors`modgunn::core::Severity`.
- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- What a gate should DO with the artifact, given the findings. Declaration
order is the strictness order — `Pass < Warn < Block`— so folding many findings into one verdict is their`Ord::max``modgunn::core::Decision`relies on).

# facett_plandag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plandag/0.1.10/facett_plandag/

## Expand description

**facett-plandag** — a **metric-bearing operator DAG**: the Spark **SQL query
plan** / Databricks **Query Profile graph**. Each node carries a multi-line
**metric body** (time / memory / rows / spill); a **cost-heat** switch
(Time / Memory / Rows) fills nodes by relative cost; **WholeStageCodegen groups**
collapse into super-nodes; and an **AQE initial-vs-final** toggle flips between
the two plan versions. The four things the doc says no single facett graph had
at once.

It **composes** facett’s existing graph stack — exactly the documented “compose
`facett_graph`, paint our own” pattern:

- `facett_graph::DepGraphView`- **column layering**+- `facett_graph::draw_arrow`
- [`facett_pipeline::Status`] supplies the**themed node-status colour**.
- The pure, serializable `model`

[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`): the resolved graph (every node’s metric body + its- **cost-heat as DATA**), the active metric/version, the collapse set, the selection.
- `Msg`- `PlanDagView::update`
- **Render-proof**: the painter and- `state_json`both read from one- `model::resolve`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use model::`- [PlanNode](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanNode.html);
- `pub use model::`- [PlanVersion](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanVersion.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- The **engine-agnostic operator-plan model**— the neutral shape a host maps a Spark**SQL query plan**/ a Databricks**Query Profile graph**/ an**AQE adaptive plan**onto, and`PlanDagView``resolve`

# facett_helix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-helix/0.1.10/facett_helix/

## Expand description

**facett-helix** — the **TIME-HELIX DAG view**. A plan / dependency DAG rendered
as a **helix that advances ALONG a time axis**: each node is a plan item (idea /
task / test / crate) tied to a `system` (its angular lane / strand); the DAG winds
*forward through time* rather than spinning in place. Edges are **soft rounded
rubberband splines** (Catmull-Rom, elastic settle); coils can be **wound onto a
pin** (`wind`); many coils coexist in one scene with **inter-helix links**; an
**animated traverse** flies a time-cursor along the axis. GPU-rendered with the
emissive **bloom** lane reused from `facett-graph3d`.

[§](https://docs.rs#portability-contract-the-reason-this-crate-exists)Portability contract (the reason this crate exists)

[ model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html) +

[depend on](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)

`layout`**nothing but**— no egui, no facett, no nornir/modgunn. They are the seam that

`serde` + `std``git mv`s into **ordning**. Only

[(this file) binds to facett’s](https://docs.rs/struct.HelixView.html)

`HelixView`[/egui/](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet``facett-graph3d`. Hosts
(nornir’s funnel, modgunn) just *populate*a

[through the](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Scene.html)

`model::Scene`[API; facett stays generic.](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanDag.html#method.add_idea)

`model::PlanDag::add_idea`[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`- `t`, angular lane, system) + the wind / level / cursor / tension — the picture asserted as DATA.
- `Msg`- `update`
- **Injected clock**(- `set_clock`- `Msg::Tick`
- **AccessKit**: each node rides into the tree as a queryable Button (FC-4).

# everruns_a2ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-a2ui/0.17.3/everruns_a2ui/

## Expand description

A2UI component catalog and prompt generator for Everruns.

Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to emit A2UI JSON component trees. The JSON is transported in ```a2ui fenced code blocks and rendered by the UI using native shadcn/ui primitives.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_a2ui::{PromptOptions, default_catalog, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_catalog(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```a2ui"));
```
Ref: specs/a2ui.md
Ref: [https://github.com/google/a2ui](https://github.com/google/a2ui)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Catalog](https://docs.rs/struct.Catalog.html)
- A catalog describes the components an agent may emit.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentCategory.html)- Category
- One category of components in a catalog (e.g. “Layout”, “Forms”).
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDef.html)- Def
- One component available to the agent.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- One prop of a component.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_catalog.html)- catalog
- The default A2UI catalog.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the default A2UI system prompt with standard options.

# everruns_openui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openui/0.17.3/everruns_openui/

## Expand description

OpenUI component library and prompt generator for Everruns.

Rust reimplementation of the OpenUI component definitions and prompt generator. Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to generate OpenUI Lang code.

The generated prompt is compatible with `@openuidev/react-lang` and `@openuidev/react-ui`
— the React runtime parses the LLM output and renders it into interactive components.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_openui::{PromptOptions, default_library, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_library(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```openui"));
```
Ref: [https://github.com/thesysdev/openui](https://github.com/thesysdev/openui)

- Component definitions: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/
- Prompt generator: packages/react-lang/src/parser/prompt.ts
- Library/types: packages/react-lang/src/library.ts

# athena_pipelines - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/athena-pipelines/3.26.3/athena_pipelines/

## Expand description

Portable Athena pipeline contracts and request-domain helpers.

This crate owns the declarative pipeline model that can be shared across the
server runtime, admin APIs, CLI/bootstrap loading, and future adapters
without depending on Actix or `AppState`.

The current scope covers:

- source/transform/sink pipeline DTOs,
- pipeline request payloads and template summaries,
- persisted template DTOs and record-to-runtime conversion helpers,
- pipeline template SQL adapters and step-log persistence helpers,
- request-independent pipeline execution orchestration behind runtime traits,
- database-backed template catalog loaders and list response contracts,
- YAML registry loading for named pipelines,
- validation and template/override resolution,
- template-name normalization and boot-template shadow policy helpers,
- gateway fetch-body construction and row alias rewriting.
- pipeline execution response contracts shared by runtime handlers and tests.

# os_display 0.1.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/os_display/0.1.4

`os_display`

This crate quotes strings so that they can be copy/pasted in the terminal.

```
use os_display::Quotable;
"filename".quote() → 'filename'
"foo'bar".quote() → "foo'bar"
"foo\u{1B}".quote() → $'foo\x1B'
"ihavenospaces".maybe_quote() → ihavenospaces
"i do have spaces".maybe_quote() → 'i do have spaces'
```
This deals with a number of problems:

-
Strings can have control codes that mess up the message or the whole terminal.
-
Whitespace and special characters must be quoted or escaped to be used in a shell command.
-
`OsString`s and`Path`s can contain invalid Unicode (which even`Path::display`

Values are rendered so that they can always be pasted back into a shell without information loss.

On Unix (and other platforms) values are quoted using bash/ksh syntax, while on Windows PowerShell syntax is used.

## When should I use this?

This crate is especially useful for command line programs that deal with arbitrary filenames or other "dirty" text. `ls` for example is the very tool you use to find odd filenames, so it's nice if it displays them well. This is why it's used in [ uutils](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils).

Another use case is printing commands for the user to run. [ xh](https://github.com/ducaale/xh) has a mode that prints

`curl` commands, using this crate to make them pretty and copy/pastable on both Unix and Windows.Any program that prints text that the user might want to paste into a terminal can get some use out of this.

Most programs get along fine without it. You likely don't strictly need it, but you may find it a nice improvement.

## Usage

Import the [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/os_display/latest/os_display/trait.Quotable.html) trait:

```
use Quotable;
```
This adds two methods to the common string types (including `OsStr`): `.quote()` and `.maybe_quote()`. They return `Quoted`, a wrapper with a custom `Display` implementation.

`.quote()` always puts quotes around the text:

```
// Found file 'filename'
println!;
// Found file "foo'bar"
println!;
// Unix: Found file $'foo\nbar'
// Windows: Found file "foo`nbar"
println!;
```
`.maybe_quote()` only adds them if necessary because of whitespace or special characters:

```
// filename: Not found
println!;
// 'foo bar': Not found
println!;
// '*?$': Not found
println!;
```
`.quote()` is best used inside longer sentences while `.maybe_quote()` can be used for text that's already separated some other way, like by a colon. This is the convention of many GNU programs.

## Limitations

- Unicode may be quoted but only control characters are escaped. The printed text can still look weird, and a few (buggy) terminals drop certain characters.
- This library should **not**be used to interpolate text into shell scripts. It's designed for readability, not absolute safety. Consider using the`shell-escape`
- The output is not compatible with every single shell.
- [Old versions of PowerShell treat quotes differently in arguments to external commands](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6714165). This library defaults to the modern behavior. The- `Quoted::external()`method toggles legacy quoting.
- I'm not a Unicode expert. The first release of this crate had multiple oversights and there may be more.

## Invalid unicode

On Unix:

```
use OsStr;
use OsStrExt;
// \xFF makes this invalid UTF-8, so to_str() would fail
let bad_string = from_bytes;
assert_eq!;
```
On Windows:

```
use OsString;
use OsStringExt;
// 0xD800 is an unpaired surrogate, making this invalid UTF-16
let bad_string = from_wide;
assert_eq!;
```
## Zero-width unicode

Some codepoints are zero-width. They can make a string invisible, or they can make it hard to select. GNU tools struggle with this:

```
$ wc $'\u200b'
wc: : No such file or directory
```
`os_display` adds quotes in such cases:

```
assert_eq!;
```
It still misleadingly looks like `''` when printed, but it's possible to copy and paste it and get the right result.

## Bidirectional unicode

A carefully-crafted string can move part of itself to the end of the line:

```
$ wc $'filename\u202E\u2066 [This does not belong!]\u2069\u2066'
wc: 'filename': No such file or directory [This does not belong!]
```
This is known as a [ Trojan Source](https://trojansource.codes/) attack. It uses control codes for bidirectional text.

`os_display` escapes those control codes if they're not properly terminated.

## Feature flags

By default you can only use the current platform's quoting style. That's appropriate most of the time.

`windows`/`unix`

The `windows` and `unix` optional features can be enabled to add constructors to `Quoted`.

`Quoted::unix("some string")` will quote with bash/ksh syntax no matter the platform, and `Quoted::windows("etc")` uses PowerShell syntax.

`Quoted::unix_raw` and `Quoted::windows_raw` take `&[u8]` (for malformed UTF-8) and `&[u16]` (for malformed UTF-16), respectively.

`native`

The `native` feature (enabled by default) is required for the `Quotable` trait and the `Quoted::native(&str)` and `Quoted::native_raw(&OsStr)` constructors. If it's not enabled then the quoting style has to be chosen explicitly.

`alloc`/`std`

This crate is `no_std`-compatible if the `alloc` and/or `std` features are disabled.

The `std` feature is required to quote `OsStr`s. The `alloc` feature is required for `Quoted::windows_raw`.

## Alternative constructors

`Quoted` has constructors for specific styles as well as `Quoted::native()` and `Quoted::native_raw()`. These can be used as an alternative to the `Quotable` trait if you prefer boring functions.

By default quotes are always added. To get behavior like `.maybe_quote()` use the `.force()` method:

```
println!;
```
## Testing

The Unix implementation has been [fuzzed](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz) against bash, zsh, mksh, ksh93 and busybox to ensure all output is interpreted back as the original string. It has been fuzzed to a more limited extent against fish, dash, tcsh, posh, and yash (which don't support all of the required syntax).

The PowerShell implementation has been fuzzed against PowerShell Core 7.1.4 running on Linux.

Both implementations have been fuzzed to test their protection against Trojan Source attacks.

## Acknowledgments

This library is modeled after the quoting done by [Gnulib](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnulib/) as seen in the GNU coreutils. The behavior is not identical, however:

- GNU uses octal escapes, like `\377`instead of`\xFF`.
- GNU eagerly switches quoting style midway through, like `''$'\n''xyz'`instead of`$'\nxyz'`.`os_display`avoids this unless necessary.
- GNU escapes unassigned codepoints instead of leaving their handling up to the terminal.
- GNU doesn't handle zero-width codepoints specially.

The first version of this code was written for the [uutils project](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils). The feedback and the opportunity to use it in a large codebase were helpful.

---

# os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/os_display/0.1.4/target-redirect/os_display/

## Expand description

Formatters for printing filenames and other strings in a terminal, with attention paid to special characters and invalid unicode.

They will wrap quotes around them and add the necessary escapes to make them copy/paste-able into a shell.

The [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html) trait adds

`quote` and `maybe_quote` methods to string
types. The [type has constructors for more explicit control.](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)

`Quoted`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;
let path = Path::new("foo/bar.baz");
// Found file 'foo/bar.baz'
println!("Found file {}", path.quote());
// foo/bar.baz: Not found
println!("{}: Not found", path.maybe_quote());
```
If the `windows`/`unix` features are enabled:

```
use os_display::Quoted;
// "foo`nbar"
println!("{}", Quoted::windows("foo\nbar"));
// $'foo\nbar'
println!("{}", Quoted::unix("foo\nbar"));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)
- A wrapper around string types for displaying with quoting and escaping applied.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html)
- An extension trait to apply quoting to strings.

---

### windows

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

[193](#193)impl Display for Quoted<'_> {
[194](#194)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
[195](#195)        match self.source {
[196](#196)            #[cfg(feature = "native")]
[197](#197)            #[cfg(feature = "std")]
[198](#198)            Kind::NativeRaw(text) => {
[199](#199)                #[cfg(unix)]
[200](#200)                use std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt;
[201](#201)                #[cfg(windows)]
[202](#202)                use std::os::windows::ffi::OsStrExt;
[203](#203)
[204](#204)                #[cfg(windows)]
[205](#205)                match text.to_str() {
[206](#206)                    Some(text) => windows::write(f, text, self.force_quote, self.external),
[207](#207)                    None => {
[208](#208)                        windows::write_escaped(f, decode_utf16(text.encode_wide()), self.external)
[209](#209)                    }
[210](#210)                }
[211](#211)                #[cfg(unix)]
[212](#212)                match text.to_str() {
[213](#213)                    Some(text) => unix::write(f, text, self.force_quote),
[214](#214)                    None => unix::write_escaped(f, text.as_bytes()),
[215](#215)                }
[216](#216)                #[cfg(not(any(windows, unix)))]
[217](#217)                match text.to_str() {
[218](#218)                    Some(text) => unix::write(f, text, self.force_quote),
[219](#219)                    None => write!(f, "{:?}", text),
[222](#222)                }
[223](#223)            }
[224](#224)
[225](#225)            #[cfg(any(feature = "unix", all(feature = "native", not(windows))))]
[226](#226)            Kind::Unix(text) => unix::write(f, text, self.force_quote),
[227](#227)
[228](#228)            #[cfg(feature = "unix")]
[229](#229)            Kind::UnixRaw(bytes) => match core::str::from_utf8(bytes) {
[230](#230)                Ok(text) => unix::write(f, text, self.force_quote),
[231](#231)                Err(_) => unix::write_escaped(f, bytes),
[232](#232)            },
[233](#233)
[234](#234)            #[cfg(any(feature = "windows", all(feature = "native", windows)))]
[235](#235)            Kind::Windows(text) => windows::write(f, text, self.force_quote, self.external),
[236](#236)
[237](#237)            #[cfg(feature = "windows")]
[238](#238)            #[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[239](#239)            Kind::WindowsRaw(units) => match alloc::string::String::from_utf16(units) {
[245](#245)                Ok(text) => windows::write(f, &text, self.force_quote, self.external),
[246](#246)                Err(_) => {
[247](#247)                    windows::write_escaped(f, decode_utf16(units.iter().cloned()), self.external)
[248](#248)                }
[249](#249)            },
[250](#250)        }
[251](#251)    }

[256](#256)fn decode_utf16(units: impl IntoIterator<Item = u16>) -> impl Iterator<Item = Result<char, u16>> {
[257](#257)    core::char::decode_utf16(units).map(|res| res.map_err(|err| err.unpaired_surrogate()))

[274](#274)fn is_bidi(ch: char) -> bool {

[279](#279)}
[280](#280)
[281](#281)#[inline(never)]
[293](#293)fn is_suspicious_bidi(text: &str) -> bool {
[294](#294)    #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
[295](#295)    enum Kind {
[296](#296)        Formatting,
[297](#297)        Isolate,
[298](#298)    }
[299](#299)    const STACK_SIZE: usize = 16;
[300](#300)    let mut stack: [Option<Kind>; STACK_SIZE] = [None; STACK_SIZE];
[302](#302)    let mut pos = 0;
[303](#303)    for ch in text.chars() {
[304](#304)        match ch {
[305](#305)            '\u{202A}' | '\u{202B}' | '\u{202D}' | '\u{202E}' => {
[306](#306)                if pos >= STACK_SIZE {
[307](#307)                    return true;
[309](#309)                }
[310](#310)                stack[pos] = Some(Kind::Formatting);
[311](#311)                pos += 1;
[312](#312)            }
[313](#313)            '\u{202C}' => {
[314](#314)                if pos == 0 {
[315](#315)                    return true;
[319](#319)                }
[320](#320)                pos -= 1;
[321](#321)                if stack[pos] != Some(Kind::Formatting) {
[322](#322)                    return true;
[326](#326)                }
[327](#327)            }
[328](#328)            '\u{2066}' | '\u{2067}' | '\u{2068}' => {
[329](#329)                if pos >= STACK_SIZE {
[330](#330)                    return true;
[331](#331)                }
[332](#332)                stack[pos] = Some(Kind::Isolate);
[333](#333)                pos += 1;
[334](#334)            }
[335](#335)            '\u{2069}' => {
[336](#336)                if pos == 0 {
[337](#337)                    return true;
[338](#338)                }
[339](#339)                pos -= 1;
[340](#340)                if stack[pos] != Some(Kind::Isolate) {
[341](#341)                    return true;
[342](#342)                }
[343](#343)            }
[344](#344)            _ => (),
[345](#345)        }
[346](#346)    }
[347](#347)    pos != 0
[348](#348)}
[349](#349)

[670](#670)        for _ in 0..n {
[671](#671)            out.push('\u{2066}');

# Quotable in os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/os_display/0.1.4/os_display/trait.Quotable.html

```
pub trait Quotable {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[quote](https://docs.rs#tymethod.quote)(&self) -> [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)<'_>;
    // Provided method
    fn [maybe_quote](https://docs.rs#method.maybe_quote)(&self) -> [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)<'_> { ... }
}## Expand description

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Returns an object that implements [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) for printing strings with
proper quoting and escaping for the platform.

On Unix this corresponds to bash/ksh syntax, on Windows PowerShell syntax is used.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;
let path = Path::new("foo/bar.baz");
println!("Found file {}", path.quote()); // Prints "Found file 'foo/bar.baz'"
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/os_display/lib.rs.html#393-397)#### fn [maybe_quote](https://docs.rs#method.maybe_quote)(&self) -> [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)<'_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/os_display/lib.rs.html#393-397)

#### fn [maybe_quote](https://docs.rs#method.maybe_quote)(&self) -> [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)<'_>

Like `quote()`, but don’t actually add quotes unless necessary because of
whitespace or special characters.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;
let foo = Path::new("foo/bar.baz");
let bar = "foo bar";
println!("{}: Not found", foo.maybe_quote()); // Prints "foo/bar.baz: Not found"
println!("{}: Not found", bar.maybe_quote()); // Prints "'foo bar': Not found"
```
```
3fn main() {
4    for arg in std::env::args_os().skip(1) {
5        println!("Native: {}", arg.maybe_quote());
6        #[cfg(all(windows, feature = "unix"))]
7        {
8            if let Some(arg) = arg.to_str() {
9                println!("Unix: {}", os_display::Quoted::unix(arg).force(false));
10            }
11        }
12        #[cfg(all(not(windows), feature = "windows"))]
13        {
14            if let Some(arg) = arg.to_str() {
15                println!("Windows: {}", os_display::Quoted::windows(arg).force(false));
16            }
17        }
18    }
19}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# Quoted in os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/os_display/0.1.4/os_display/struct.Quoted.html

`pub struct Quoted<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A wrapper around string types for displaying with quoting and escaping applied.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Quote a string with the default style for the platform.

On Windows this is PowerShell syntax, on all other platforms this is bash/ksh syntax.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/os_display/lib.rs.html#113-115)#### pub fn [native_raw](https://docs.rs#method.native_raw)(text: &'a [OsStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsStr.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/os_display/lib.rs.html#113-115)

#### pub fn [native_raw](https://docs.rs#method.native_raw)(text: &'a [OsStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsStr.html)) -> Self

Quote an `OsStr` with the default style for the platform.

On platforms other than Windows and Unix, if the encoding is
invalid, the `Debug` representation will be used.

```
3fn main() {
4    for arg in std::env::args_os().skip(1) {
5        println!("Native: {}", arg.maybe_quote());
6        #[cfg(all(windows, feature = "unix"))]
7        {
8            if let Some(arg) = arg.to_str() {
9                println!("Unix: {}", os_display::Quoted::unix(arg).force(false));
10            }
11        }
12        #[cfg(all(not(windows), feature = "windows"))]
13        {
14            if let Some(arg) = arg.to_str() {
15                println!("Windows: {}", os_display::Quoted::windows(arg).force(false));
16            }
17        }
18    }
19}
```
Toggle forced quoting. If `true`, quotes are added even if no special
characters are present.

Defaults to `true`.

```
3fn main() {
4    for arg in std::env::args_os().skip(1) {
5        println!("Native: {}", arg.maybe_quote());
6        #[cfg(all(windows, feature = "unix"))]
7        {
8            if let Some(arg) = arg.to_str() {
9                println!("Unix: {}", os_display::Quoted::unix(arg).force(false));
10            }
11        }
12        #[cfg(all(not(windows), feature = "windows"))]
13        {
14            if let Some(arg) = arg.to_str() {
15                println!("Windows: {}", os_display::Quoted::windows(arg).force(false));
16            }
17        }
18    }
19}
```
When quoting for PowerShell, toggle whether to use legacy quoting for external programs.

If enabled, double quotes (and sometimes backslashes) will be escaped so
that they can be passed to external programs in PowerShell versions before
7.3, or with `$PSNativeCommandArgumentPassing` set to `'Legacy'`.

If disabled, quoting will suit modern argument passing (always used for internal commandlets and .NET functions). Strings that look like options or numbers will be quoted.

It is sadly impossible to quote a string such that it’s suitable for both modern and legacy argument passing.

Defaults to `false`.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-4)Optional

This requires either the `windows` or the `native` feature. It has no effect
on Unix-style quoting.

# os_display - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/os_display/latest/os_display/

## Expand description

Formatters for printing filenames and other strings in a terminal, with attention paid to special characters and invalid unicode.

They will wrap quotes around them and add the necessary escapes to make them copy/paste-able into a shell.

The [ Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html) trait adds

`quote` and `maybe_quote` methods to string
types. The [type has constructors for more explicit control.](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)

`Quoted`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::path::Path;
use os_display::Quotable;
let path = Path::new("foo/bar.baz");
// Found file 'foo/bar.baz'
println!("Found file {}", path.quote());
// foo/bar.baz: Not found
println!("{}: Not found", path.maybe_quote());
```
If the `windows`/`unix` features are enabled:

```
use os_display::Quoted;
// "foo`nbar"
println!("{}", Quoted::windows("foo\nbar"));
// $'foo\nbar'
println!("{}", Quoted::unix("foo\nbar"));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Quoted](https://docs.rs/struct.Quoted.html)
- A wrapper around string types for displaying with quoting and escaping applied.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Quotable](https://docs.rs/trait.Quotable.html)
- An extension trait to apply quoting to strings.

---

# unicode-width 0.2.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unicode-width/^0.2.0

`unicode-width`

Determine displayed width of `char` and `str` types according to [Unicode Standard Annex #11](http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr11/)
and other portions of the Unicode standard.

This crate is `#![no_std]`.

```
use UnicodeWidthStr;
```
**NOTE:** The computed width values may not match the actual rendered column
width. For example, many Brahmic scripts like Devanagari have complex rendering rules
which this crate does not currently handle (and will never fully handle, because
the exact rendering depends on the font):

```
extern crate unicode_width;
use UnicodeWidthStr;
```
Additionally, [defective combining character sequences](https://unicode.org/glossary/#defective_combining_character_sequence)
and nonstandard [Korean jamo](https://unicode.org/glossary/#jamo) sequences may
be rendered with a different width than what this crate says. (This is not an
exhaustive list.) For a list of what this crate *does* handle, see
[docs.rs](https://docs.rs/unicode-width/latest/unicode_width/#rules-for-determining-width).

## crates.io

You can use this package in your project by adding the following
to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Changelog

### 0.2.0

- Treat `\n`as width 1 (#60)
- Treat ambiguous `Modifier_Letter`s as narrow (#63)
- Support `Grapheme_Cluster_Break=Prepend`(#62)
- Support lots of ligatures (#53)

Note: If you are using `unicode-width` for linebreaking, the change treating `\n` as width 1 *may cause behavior changes*. It is recommended that in such cases you feed already-line segmented text to `unicode-width`. In other words, please apply higher level control character based line breaking protocols before feeding text to `unicode-width`. Relying on any character producing a stable width in this crate is likely the sign of a bug.

---

# os_display 0.1.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/os_display/0.1.3

`os_display`

Printing strings can be tricky. They may contain control codes that mess up the message or the whole terminal. On Unix even filenames can contain characters like that.

Filenames may also contain invalid unicode, which is not preserved by [ Path::display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/path/struct.Path.html#method.display).

Finally, they can contain special characters that aren't safe to use in a command without quoting or escaping.

This library lets you add quoting to filenames (and other strings) to display them more safely and usefully. The goal is to render them in such a way that they can be copied and pasted back into a shell without information loss.

On Unix (and other platforms) values are quoted using bash/ksh syntax, while on Windows PowerShell syntax is used.

## When should I use this?

This library is best suited for command line programs that deal with arbitrary filenames or other "dirty" text. `mv` for example is the very tool you use to rename files with problematic names, so it's nice if its messages handle them well.

Programs that aren't expected to deal with weird data don't get as much benefit.

The output is made for shells, so displaying it in e.g. a GUI may not make sense.

Most programs get along fine without this. You likely don't strictly need it, but you may find it a nice improvement.

## Usage

Import the `Quotable` trait:

```
use Quotable;
```
This adds two methods to the common string types (including `OsStr`): `.quote()` and `.maybe_quote()`. They return `Quoted`, a wrapper with a custom `Display` implementation.

`.quote()` always puts quotes around the text:

```
// Found file 'filename'
println!;
// Found file "foo'bar"
println!;
// Unix: Found file $'foo\nbar'
// Windows: Found file "foo`nbar"
println!;
```
`.maybe_quote()` only adds them if necessary because of whitespace or special characters:

```
// filename: Not found
println!;
// 'foo bar': Not found
println!;
// '*?$': Not found
println!;
```
`.quote()` is best used inside longer sentences while `.maybe_quote()` can be used for text that's already separated some other way (like by a colon).

## Limitations

- Unicode may be quoted but only control characters are escaped. The printed text can still look weird, and a few (buggy) terminals drop certain characters.
- This library should **not**be used to interpolate text into shell scripts. It's designed for readability, not absolute safety. Consider using the`shell-escape`
- The output is not compatible with every single shell.
- [PowerShell treats quotes differently in arguments to external commands](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6714165). This library defaults to quoting for internal commandlets, which may not be what you want. The- `Quoted::external()`method toggles this.
- I'm not a Unicode expert. The first release of this crate had multiple oversights and there may be more.

## Invalid unicode

On Unix:

```
use OsStr;
use OsStrExt;
// \xFF makes this invalid UTF-8, so to_str() would fail
let bad_string = from_bytes;
assert_eq!;
```
On Windows:

```
use OsString;
use OsStringExt;
// 0xD800 is an unpaired surrogate, making this invalid UTF-16
let bad_string = from_wide;
assert_eq!;
```
## Zero-width unicode

Some codepoints are zero-width. They can make a string invisible, or they can make it hard to select. GNU tools struggle with this:

```
$ wc $'\u200b'
wc: : No such file or directory
```
`os_display` adds quotes in such cases:

```
assert_eq!;
```
It still misleadingly looks like `''` when printed, but it's possible to copy and paste it and get the right result.

## Bidirectional unicode

A carefully-crafted string can move part of itself to the end of the line:

```
$ wc $'filename\u202E\u2066 [This does not belong!]\u2069\u2066'
wc: 'filename': No such file or directory [This does not belong!]
```
This is known as a [ Trojan Source](https://trojansource.codes/) attack. It uses control codes for bidirectional text.

`os_display` escapes those control codes if they're not properly terminated.

## Feature flags

By default you can only use the current platform's quoting style. That's appropriate most of the time.

`windows`/`unix`

The `windows` and `unix` optional features can be enabled to add constructors to `Quoted`.

`Quoted::unix("some string")` will quote with bash/ksh syntax no matter the platform, and `Quoted::windows("etc")` uses PowerShell syntax.

`Quoted::unix_raw` and `Quoted::windows_raw` take `&[u8]` (for malformed UTF-8) and `&[u16]` (for malformed UTF-16), respectively.

`native`

The `native` feature (enabled by default) is required for the `Quotable` trait and the `Quoted::native(&str)` and `Quoted::native_raw(&OsStr)` constructors. If it's not enabled then the quoting style has to be chosen explicitly.

`alloc`/`std`

This crate is `no_std`-compatible if the `alloc` and/or `std` features are disabled.

The `std` feature is required to quote `OsStr`s. The `alloc` feature is required for `Quoted::windows_raw`.

## Alternative constructors

`Quoted` has constructors for specific styles as well as `Quoted::native()` and `Quoted::native_raw()`. These can be used as an alternative to the `Quotable` trait if you prefer boring functions.

By default quotes are always added. To get behavior like `.maybe_quote()` use the `.force()` method:

```
println!;
```
## Testing

The Unix implementation has been [fuzzed](https://github.com/rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz) against bash, zsh, mksh, ksh93 and busybox to ensure all output is interpreted back as the original string. It has been fuzzed to a more limited extent against fish, dash, tcsh, posh, and yash (which don't support all of the required syntax).

The PowerShell implementation has been fuzzed against PowerShell Core 7.1.4 running on Linux.

Both implementations have been fuzzed to test their protection against Trojan Source attacks.

## Acknowledgments

This library is modeled after the quoting done by [Gnulib](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnulib/) as seen in the GNU coreutils. The behavior is not identical, however:

- GNU uses octal escapes, like `\377`instead of`\xFF`.
- GNU eagerly switches quoting style midway through, like `''$'\n''xyz'`instead of`$'\nxyz'`.`os_display`avoids this unless necessary.
- GNU escapes unassigned codepoints instead of leaving their handling up to the terminal.
- GNU doesn't handle zero-width codepoints specially.

The first version of this code was written for the [uutils project](https://github.com/uutils/coreutils). The feedback and the opportunity to use it in a large codebase were helpful.

---
